title: Out of the woods: psychophysiological investigations on wood odors to estimate their suitability as ambient scents
research_question: To assess the subjective evaluation of, and physiological responses to, wood odors and individual wood odor constituents to estimate their suitability as ambient scents and understand their influence on human well-being and mood.

participants.description: Twenty healthy women (mean age=29±9 years) participated. All were right-handers and passed the MoCA test (average±SD: 28.7±1.6). Exclusion criteria included smoking, pregnancy, age under 18 or above 40, and allergies.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies volunteers who gave informed consent.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five odor stimuli and one odorless control: cedar wood oil (10% solution in propylene glycol), pine needles oil (10% solution in propylene glycol), α-pinene (0.5% solution in propylene glycol), thymoquinone (0.5% solution in propylene glycol, absorbed on fiber material in a plastic jar), lavender oil (5% solution in propylene glycol), and water (odorless control). Odors were presented for 2s via an olfactometer with respiration-triggered onset.

measures.instrument: 10-point visual analogue scale (0=no perception to 10=strong perception)
10-point visual analogue scale (0=very unpleasant to 10=very pleasant)
10-point visual analogue scale (0=not at all to 10=extremely)
10-point visual analogue scale (0=not at all to 10=extremely) for 'alert', 'active', 'calm', 'relaxed' feelings
10-point visual analogue scale (0=not at all to 10=extremely) for 'happy', 'content' feelings
GSR Amp FE116, GSR Finger Electrodes, analyzed with Ledalab (V.3.4.9) for integrated skin conductance response (ISCR)
Piezo-electric pulse transducer (TN1012/ST), difference scores (8s poststimulus – 1s prestimulus)
Skin temperature probe (MLT422/A, MLT409/A), thermistor pod (ML309), difference scores (8s poststimulus – 1s prestimulus)

mechanisms: Qualitative differences in wood odors lead to different pleasantness percepts.
Different odor intensities might enhance stimulus relevance or entail different sniffing behavior.
Heart rate increases with happiness (arousal/affective response).
implementation_implications: Wood odors can be purposefully used to promote human well-being and recovery from stressful situations.
Wood odors can be used in various environmental settings (home, public transportation, shops) to enhance comfort and relaxation.
Careful selection of wood odors is necessary to achieve desired outcomes.
α-pinene is a potent individual odor-active compound for enhancing subjective mood, comparable to or more potent than complex natural wood odors.
Pine needle odor and α-pinene are promising odor stimuli for long-term exposure in odor-enhanced environments.
Specific wood odors and odorants can be used as room scents to influence human behavior by enhancing mood and restoration.

tables.description: Medians of subjective evaluations of perceived activation and mood, and median heart rate (HR), skin conductance (ISCR), and finger temperature (FT) responses to the six stimuli, along with the p-value of the Friedman test.
Spearman correlations between physiological measurements (FT change, HR change, ISCR) and subjective evaluations, calculated for the individual odors.

limitations: Pleasantness ratings of presented odors were in a narrow range (3 to 6), potentially limiting physiological measures as indicators of subjective pleasantness.
Physiological responses to olfactory events did not significantly differentiate stimuli, providing limited information on wood odor perception.
The experimental procedure (immediate effects of short-term exposure) may not accurately estimate psychophysiological effects in long-term environmental exposure situations (e.g., room scents).
The study focused on olfactory stimuli as sole stimuli, not in combination with congruent auditory or visual stimuli.
Stress was not induced in participants, limiting the assessment of wood odors' potential for stress recovery.

paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractWood has been an important raw material for centuries, and humans encounter it in the form of furniture and building materials or in products of daily use. The odors emanating from such wood-based materials can add another facet to their functionality by influencing human well-being and mood. Moreover, wood odors can be used in odor-enhanced environments to foster relaxation and stress recovery. The current study was conducted to assess the subjective evaluation of, and physiological responses to, wood odors and individual wood odor constituents. The subjects smelled the odors of pine needles oil, cedar wood oil, α-pinene, and thymoquinone and evaluated the odor percept and their subjective feelings. Heart rate, finger temperature, and skin conductance were monitored throughout the experiment. The results showed that wood odors were distinct regarding their pleasantness, familiarity, and intensity. All odors enhanced the subjective feelings of happiness and content. Though no odor-specific physiological effects became evident, certain physiological measures correlated with self-reports of happy and relaxed feelings and the intensity ratings of the odors. The present study provides a basis for further studies on the use of wood odors as ambient scents and helps understanding the influence of natural odors on humans.
